newsitem.title: PERU: Inca Cola replaces Che on "pacified" Lima campus.
newsitem.headline: Inca Cola replaces Che on "pacified" Lima campus.

text.p: "Young student: As a soldier, I am here to support and protect you in your career. Trust in me," reads a banner at San Marcos University, where young Peruvian conscripts with rifles lean on sandbags.
The dining hall at the modern campus of Latin America's oldest university used to be daubed with huge graffiti of the Peruvian Communist Party and boil with left-wing fervor.

Across the campus, the Law Faculty that once bragged a life-sized statue of revolutionary hero Ernesto "Che" Guevara now has an Inca Cola vending machine at the entrance instead. Trees around which students used to dance to Andean folk music are painted in military-style white and smart green rubbish bins proclaim "Cleanliness is Culture."

President Alberto Fujimori's "pacification" of Peru has banished politics from a university that was once a cradle of revolt and stronghold of guerrillas from the Maoist Shining Path to the Marxist Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).

Protected for years by the autonomy of state universities, which put them out of bounds to police, Shining Path and MRTA militants used the classrooms for indoctrination, sang rebel hymns and sometimes terrorised other students and teachers. Their disappearance from the campus on Lima's outskirts is one of Fujimori's victories against guerrilla violence, which cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in damage over nearly 17 years.

Today's students are apparently indifferent to continuing insurgence, dramatised by the MRTA's two-month-old siege of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, where they are holding 72 hostages to demand the release of jailed comrades.
For some students, the "reorganization" of state campuses that began in 1991 when Fujimori first sent in the troops is a welcome end to the strikes, riots and anarchy of the 1980s.

"Now the university is cleaner, the classes are more regular and there is more control," an economics student said, recalling that when he started studying in 1987 rebels would interrupt classes for political harangues, protests and occasionally even shootouts with rival factions.

For others, the wholesale expulsion of politicized student leaders and teachers who used the campus as a sanctuary has gone too far, creating a sterile atmosphere where intelligent political debate is dead.

"It used to be a pigsty. Now it looks like a hospital," one 1988 graduate said, surveying whitewashed walls that were covered in her day by murals of Chairman Mao and Tupac Amaru, the Indian nobleman who revolted against Spanish rule in 1782, and Abimael Guzman, the Shining Path leader arrested in 1992.
Guzman is a former academic himself, once a philosophy professor at Huamanga University in Ayacucho, the Shining Path's highland stronghold.

In 1991, when San Marcos celebrated its 440th birthday, Fujimori, a former university rector, enraged students by sending in 2,000 soldiers to scrape graffiti off the walls. Typically, he joined the troops for the clean-up.

In 1995, believing state universities were still "the refuge of terrorists," he pushed a law through Congress setting up "reorganization committees" that are still in charge. Out went the "eternal students" who often stretched their studies for more than a decade and who were prime suspects of insurgency. In went the troops -- to stay.

"Student leaders don't talk about politics any more because they're scared," a 22-year-old psychology student said. "Now the graffiti says things like 'Norma loves Eric' and you hardly see 'Shining Path' or 'MRTA'. Students have lost their critical spirit. Now all they talk about is parties, girls, money and status symbols."

Fabian, a 23-year-old physics graduate, says new fees mean opportunities to study for youngsters from the teeming slums around Lima have been reduced and students are more likely to be middle-class and apolitical. "They've thrown out a lot of politicized students and what's left is an indifferent youth."
